title: Trending — A 5.3-million-year-old deep-sea whale necropolis in the Diamantina Zone
one_line: A 2023 crewed-submersible survey of the Diamantina Zone (4,616–7,001 m, SE Indian Ocean) documented 485 whale sites — 5 active whale falls and 476 fossil cetaceans — spread over ~1,200 km of seafloor, with strontium dating pushing whale-fall deposition back to at least 5.26 Ma.
key_claims: Five modern whale-fall communities were found in the sulfur-philic stage, the deepest at 6,789 m, far beyond the previous ~4,200 m record, with organism densities up to 2,840 individuals per square metre dominated by Osedax bone-boring worms, chemosynthetic bivalves and brittle stars.
Strontium isotope dating of 33 fossil specimens gave ages from 120,000 years to 5.26 million years, indicating continuous whale-fall deposition since the early Pliocene.
The fossil assemblage is dominated by deep-diving beaked whales (Ziphiidae), including extant species and a newly described extinct species, Pterocetus diamantinae (oldest specimen).

Authors propose a 'super corridor': an estimated ~8 whale falls per square kilometre across 1,200 km provides stepping stones for larval dispersal between falls and onward to vents and seeps, supported by shared gastropod and squat lobster taxa.
Preservation is attributed to ultra-low sedimentation (<0.5 cm per 1,000 years), ferromanganese oxide coating, and pachyosteosclerotic beaked whale rostra resisting boring and dissolution.
limitations: Only a single chemosynthetic bivalve (genus Southwardia per the episode) could be confidently matched to existing sequence databases; most fauna remain undescribed.
Ages derive from strontium isotope ratios in bone mineral matched to a seawater curve rather than direct radiometric dating of the carcasses.
The proposed lethal-dive mechanism rests on modelled ~3,000 m maximum safe beaked whale dive depth plus trench topography, not on direct observation of mortality events.
The super corridor is an inference from fall density and shared taxa; no larval dispersal or connectivity was directly measured.
Only a subset of fossils (33 dated, ~43 recovered per the discussion) was analysed out of 476 recorded sites, and only one trench region was surveyed.
open_questions: Do population-genetic or larval-tracking data confirm connectivity between adjacent whale falls and with nearby vent and seep systems?
Are comparable ultra-deep organic-fall accumulations present in other under-mapped hadal trenches, or is the Diamantina Zone unique?
Can tagging or carcass observations confirm that fatal over-deep foraging dives, rather than other mortality, generate the beaked whale concentration?
What morphological or molecular series can the fossil archive yield to reconstruct beaked whale evolution across the 5.26-Myr record?
